claims.text: Formation and persistence of a protective oxide on CrFeCoNiX above 900 °C are governed by alloy composition.
The Cr-to-Fe ratio governs oxidation behavior and protective-oxide persistence.
The identity and content of X, where X is Si, Mn, or Al, govern oxidation behavior and protective-oxide persistence.
Composition affects surface-oxide structural evolution by controlling atomic size, redox potential, and compositional segregation.
Compositional segregation and surface-oxide structural evolution mediate the response to high-temperature oxidative or corrosive exposure.
Atomic size, redox potential, and compositional segregation control oxidation behavior.
An optimal Cr-to-Fe ratio and X content will produce a stable, coherent, slow-growing oxide that persists above 900 °C.
Some CrFeCoNiX alloys develop unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation.
Some CrMoTiAlY alloys, with Y equal to Ta, Nb, or W, develop unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation.
The hypothesis applies to CrFeCoNiX alloys in single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution states.
The proposed service boundary is 900–1000 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere.
Oxide thickness, oxide composition, surface-oxide structural evolution, and compositional segregation can be used to test the hypothesis.
